name: Kudamadu Koothan Temple, Thiruarimeya Vinnagaram
deity: Krishna as Kudamadu Koothan, the Lord who danced with pots, with the Goddess Amruthagadavalli — a Thirunangur Divya Desam
period: A Divya Desam of Chola Nadu and one of the eleven Thirunangur Tirupathis, sung by Thirumangai Alvar in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham
dynasty: Chola country of the Alvar era (no patron recorded)
summary: At Thiruarimeya Vinnagaram in Thirunangur, Vishnu is worshipped as Kudamadu Koothan, the pot-dancing Krishna, with Amruthagadavalli — a stucco image anointed with oil alone, sung by Thirumangai Alvar in one decad.

sections.history: Thiruarimeya Vinnagaram, known locally simply as Kudamadu Koothar Kovil, stands in the village of Thirunangur near Sirkazhi in Chola Nadu. It is one of the 108 Divya Desams sung by the Alvars in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, and one of the eleven Thirunangur Tirupathis. Thirumangai Alvar devoted a full decad of ten pasurams to it, Periya Thirumozhi 3.10. The presiding Lord is Kudamadu Koothan, Krishna, with the Goddess Amruthagadavalli. No inscription or royal patron is firmly recorded, so the shrine's age rests on the hymns, placed between the seventh and ninth centuries.
sections.architecture: A Dravidian temple whose sanctum is crowned by the Ucchasrunga vimana. Its sacred tank is the Koti Amrutha Theertham. The central image is unusual in its making: the Lord is a sudai image, of stucco or burnt clay, rather than carved stone. For this reason it is anointed only with oil, the thailakappu, and never with water, a custom that shapes the daily worship here.
sections.legends: The name Kudamadu Koothan, the Lord who dances with pots, recalls the kudakoothu, Krishna's dance with pots at Gokulam in the tales of his childhood. Another telling links the name with Govardhana, the hill the young Krishna held aloft as an umbrella over the cowherds. These are the traditions that gather round the name; the shrine itself is counted among the eleven forms in which Vishnu is said to have appeared at Thirunangur.
sections.festivals: The shrine joins the Garuda Sevai on the day after Thai Amavasai (January–February), when its utsavar is taken on a Garuda vahana to Thirumanimadam to meet the other ten lords of Thirunangur, and the Mangalasasana Utsavam recalls Thirumangai Alvar's hymns. Tradition holds that seeing all eleven together equals visiting each one.
sections.experience: Come for the Krishna of the pot-dance, and for the rare chance to see a stucco image tended with oil alone. Read the decad of Periya Thirumozhi 3.10 before you set out if you can. The temple is small and quiet, among paddy fields about 10 km by road from Sirkazhi.

visit.timings: Darshan is generally held in morning and evening sessions with a midday break; the Garuda Sevai day is by far the busiest. Confirm timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Thirunangur lies about 10 km by road south-east of Sirkazhi (Sirkali) in Mayiladuthurai district. Sirkazhi, on the Chennai–Mayiladuthurai railway line, is the nearest station, and Tiruchirappalli, about 160 km away, the nearest major airport. Auto-rickshaws and taxis from Sirkazhi reach the village; the eleven shrines lie among paddy fields close to one another.
